author: Tim
title: Marathon Legend Passes Away At 114
text:
Fauja Singh, believed to be the world’s oldest marathon runner, has died at 114. Reports say he was hit by a car while crossing the road in his village in Punjab, India.
The accident happened on Monday in Beas Pind, near where he lived. He passed away from injuries related to the crash. Singh became famous late in life. He didn’t start running marathons until he was 89.
Over the years, he racked up a list of honors. He got a letter from Queen Elizabeth II, appeared in the Guinness Book of World Records, and even carried the Olympic torch in 2012.
He moved to Ilford in 1992 and was well known in the local community there. His running club, Sikhs In The City, was based in London.
The club confirmed his death and called him an “icon of humanity and powerhouse of positivity.” They said: “He succumbed to injuries caused by a vehicle accident while crossing the road close to his home.”
They also shared how they plan to honor him. “His running club and charity Sikhs In The City will be devoting all of its events until the Fauja Singh Birthday Challenge on Sunday 29 March 2026 to celebrate his life of success and achievements,” they wrote.
They continued: “We will be doubling the efforts to raise funds to building the Fauja Singh Clubhouse on the route in Ilford where he used to train.”
“In lieu of flowers please donate to his Clubhouse Appeal so we can carry on his legacy to encourage the world to keep fit and stay positive,” the post said.
Singh got into running after his wife passed away in 2000. It started as something to cope with grief but turned into something much bigger.
At 90, he ran the London Marathon in six hours and 54 minutes. That beat the previous record for anyone over 90 by nearly an hour. He didn’t stop there. His best time came in 2003 at the Toronto Waterfront Marathon, where he finished in five hours and 40 minutes.
Even after turning 100, he kept going. In 2011, he tried to become the first 100-year-old to officially finish a marathon. The Guinness World Records said it was an “inspirational achievement,” but they couldn’t count it officially because of issues with his birth certificate.
He retired from racing at age 101 but remained a symbol of determination and hope.
